newsitem.title: RWANDA: 460,000 Rwandan refugees back from Tanzania-U.N..
newsitem.headline: 460,000 Rwandan refugees back from Tanzania-U.N..

text.p: Some 460,000 Rwandan refugees have returned to Rwanda from Tanzania before a Tanzanian deadline of Tuesday for all 540,000 to leave, the U.N. refugee agency said on Saturday.
Paul Stromberg, a spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), said more than 21,500 refugees crossed from northwestern Tanzania to Rwanda on Friday, most of them on trucks.
"This takes the total in December to about 460,000. Today we expect them to continue with the last big group of refugees from the Karagwe camps crossing either today or on Sunday," he said.
"After that we expect smaller groups to keep arriving."

He said Tanzanian authorities detained more than 50 Rwandans from camps around the northwestern town of Ngara and perhaps 100 from the Karagwe camps. UNHCR was in contact with officials over what would happen to the detainees and their families, he added.
Troops and police stopped hundreds of thousands of refugees from fleeing deeper into Tanzania. U.N. officials said they had reports some refugees were brutally treated to force them home.

The December 31 deadline set by the Tanzanian government for all 540,000 Rwandan refugees to leave followed the return of an estimated 600,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees from eastern Zaire after they were forced out of their camps in October and November.
The Hutu refugees in Tanzania and Zaire fled from Rwanda in 1994 after some took part in the genocide of about 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus.

Rwanda's first genocide trial opened in the southeastern town of Kibungo on Friday with the two accused facing the death penalty if they are convicted of taking part in the genocide. Neither of the accused in Kibungo has defence lawyers.
Large numbers of refugees in eastern Zaire fled deeper into the country rather than return to Rwanda.
A UNHCR mission to eastern Zaire on December 18-20 found as many as 270,000 Rwandan refugees at Tingi-Tingi and around the eastern town of Shabunda and aid agencies are struggling to reach them.
"The problem is the sites are practically inaccessible. Some areas are only reached by dug-out canoes and bicycles. So the problem is how to get aid in before anything else," Stromberg said.
